blocks.text: 我们使用缩放阶梯来评估模型改动，缩放阶梯是一组采用固定训练配方、规模不同的模型。阶梯的每一级以其层数 \( L \) 命名，仅由 \( L \) 决定架构的其余部分。例如，隐藏维度为 \( (256/3) \cdot L \)，查询头数为 \( L \)，并四舍五入到最接近的 16 的倍数。我们在保持每个活跃参数的训练 token 数（TPP）不变的情况下，训练规模递增的模型。

blocks.text: 为了在较小规模下考虑多轮训练，我们使用了一种称为源缩放的技术。在缩放阶梯的较低层级，源缩放人为限制模型训练所用的唯一样本集合，使得无论训练时长如何，每个数据集都重复相同的次数。例如，如果一个数据集在完整的 50T token 训练中重复 8 次，那么 5T token 的训练将仅对该数据的 1/10 循环 8 次。

blocks.text: 我们联合扫描学习率（\(LR\)）和权重衰减（\(WD\)），因为它们对训练的影响是耦合的。模型性能对 \(LR\) 与 \(WD\) 的乘积最为敏感，因此好的配置位于 \((\log{LR}, \log{WD})\) 平面上一条狭窄的对角带内。在 \((\log{LR}, \log{WD})\) 中做矩形网格采样会低效地覆盖这条带，因此我们改为在 \((\log{LR}, \log{(LR \times WD)})\) 中扫描网格。

blocks.text: 协同设计我们的基础设施与 MAI-Base-2

inlines.text: 协同设计我们的基础设施与 MAI-Base-2

blocks.text: 在计算预算内训练前沿模型，需要针对评估质量和计算效率协同设计模型与基础设施。我们使用效率增益（EG）指标来帮助指导决策：候选方案达到与基线相同评估损失所需计算量的比值。计算量可以用 FLOPs（EGFLOPs）或墙钟时间（EGtime）衡量，两者互补。我们主要依赖 EGtime，因为它反映了我们基础设施的当前状态。而 EGFLOPs则衡量原型的潜力，并指导未来的基础设施开发：一项在 FLOPs 上胜出但在墙钟时间上落败的改动，会告诉我们该在哪里投入。这种建模与基础设施的联合优化体现在以下若干设计选择中。

blocks.text: 扩展 MoE

blocks.text: 减少每专家开销

inlines.text: 减少每专家开销

blocks.text: 我们通过四种方式减少每个专家的开销。首先，我们通过对每个专家组同时分组计算和通信，提升 GEMM 和 NVLink 效率。这减少了内核启动开销和长尾效应。其次，我们通过使用驻留在设备上的 token 元数据并直接从 GPU 发起 all-to-all 通信，减少主机-设备同步。第三，我们进一步利用对称内存优化 all-to-all，直接在 NVLink 上交换 token，无需暂存拷贝，从而提升通信吞吐量，并在并发运行 GEMM 时减少 HBM 争用。最后，我们跨层批量处理负载均衡损失，用一次跨所有层的批量归约替代逐层的 all-reduce。这些优化使我们能够训练更稀疏的模型，而不会显著降低 MFU。

inlines.text: 扩展 Muon

blocks.text: 在扩展到 MAI-Base-2 时，我们发现 Muon 相比 AdamW 带来了更稳定的训练动态和大幅效率提升。将 Muon 用于我们最大的模型，需要降低其每步开销。

inlines.text: 在扩展到 MAI-Base-2 时，我们发现 Muon 相比 AdamW 带来了更稳定的训练动态和大幅效率提升。将 Muon 用于我们最大的模型，需要降低其每步开销。

blocks.text: Muon 使用 Newton–Schulz 对每个权重矩阵的动量进行正交化，这是一种由若干矩阵乘法组成的迭代算法。这需要完整矩阵，与 ZeRO 在数据并行维度上对动量进行分片相冲突。遵循先前工作，我们在优化器步骤中重新分片动量。每个 GPU 更新其本地 FP32 动量分片并将其转换为 BF16。随后，对相同形状的参数进行批量 all-to-all 交换，使每个 GPU 拥有完整动量矩阵的一个子集。每个 GPU 使用对称感知的 Newton–Schulz 内核在本地对其完整动量矩阵进行正交化。第二次 all-to-all 将更新返回到其原始分片，在那里它们被转换回 FP32 并应用于权重。

我们通过预取多个批次来重叠通信和计算。

blocks.text: 激活梯度裁剪

inlines.text: 激活梯度裁剪

blocks.text: 梯度裁剪是一种通过降低离群梯度影响来稳定训练的常用方法。标准梯度裁剪作用于整个批次权重梯度的全局范数。然而，离群梯度通常由批次中一小部分数据驱动。因此，一个离群样本可能导致整个批次的梯度被缩小，包括那些表现良好的样本的贡献。作为一种更有针对性的缓解措施，我们在网络中的选定位置对激活值梯度进行裁剪。结合 Muon，这使 MAI-Base-2 的梯度范数保持在比 MAI-Base-1 更紧的范围内（图 7）。

blocks.text: Robust scaling ladders

inlines.text: Robust scaling ladders

blocks.text: We evaluate model changes using a scaling ladder, a family of models of different sizes with a fixed training recipe. Each rung of the ladder is named after its number of layers \( L \), and \( L \) alone determines the rest of the architecture. For example, the hidden size is \( (256/3) \cdot L \), and the number of query heads is \( L \), rounded to the nearest multiple of 16. We train models of increasing size while holding training tokens per active parameter (TPP) constant.

blocks.text: To account for multi-epoch training at smaller scales, we use a technique we call source scaling. On the lower rungs of the scaling ladder, source scaling artificially restricts the set of unique samples the model trains on, so that each dataset is repeated the same number of times regardless of the training horizon. For example, if a dataset is repeated 8 times over the full 50T-token run, a 5T-token run will loop 8 times over just 1/10 of that data.

blocks.text: Direct comparisons between models conflate the quality of the training recipe with differences in model size and training compute. To isolate the recipe, we estimate how much compute our recipe would need to match a strong external base model. We use DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base as the reference: it is the only released base pretraining checkpoint with more than one trillion parameters, though it is still trained on significantly fewer FLOPs than MAI-Base-2.

blocks.text: Codesigning our infrastructure and MAI-Base-2

inlines.text: Codesigning our infrastructure and MAI-Base-2

blocks.text: Training frontier models within a compute budget requires co-designing models and infrastructure for both evaluation quality and computational efficiency. We use an efficiency gain (EG) metric to help guide our decisions: the ratio of compute required by a candidate to reach the same evaluation loss as the baseline. Compute can be measured in FLOPs (EGFLOPs) or in wall-clock time (EGtime), and the two are complementary. We rely mainly on EGtime, since it reflects the current state of our infrastructure. EGFLOPs, in turn, measures a prototype’s potential and guides future infrastructure development: a change that wins on FLOPs but loses on wall-clock time shows us where to invest. This joint optimization of modeling and infrastructure is reflected in several design choices below.

blocks.text: Dropless MoE with tunable, fixed-size memory usage

inlines.text: Dropless MoE with tunable, fixed-size memory usage

blocks.text: In MoE layers, each expert sees a variable number of tokens. This introduces GPU memory challenges as experts that are overloaded can run out of memory. One solution is to set a fixed threshold for each expert, after which additional tokens are dropped. Our experiments found that dropping tokens leads to worse performance. A naive solution is to simply allocate enough memory per expert to account for the largest imbalance, but this leads to inefficient usage of memory under normal loads. Our multi-round dropless MoE, illustrated in Figure 6, achieves fixed memory usage under arbitrary routing imbalance, eliminating fragmentation and out-of-memory crashes.

blocks.text: We group the experts on each expert parallel rank into one or more groups of a configurable size. Each expert group runs one or more dispatch → compute → collect rounds with a fixed per-expert token capacity. If an expert receives more tokens than it can hold, the expert group processes those overflow tokens in additional rounds. To reduce the number of additional rounds, we allow overloaded experts to use unused token capacity from other experts in the same group. In the backward pass, we then perform fine-grained recomputation per expert group following a similar multi-round schedule. This keeps memory usage static regardless of token imbalance. Token capacity is configurable: more capacity means more memory, and less capacity means potentially more rounds and thus extra compute. In practice, the capacity is configured to maintain a single round in steady state.

blocks.text: Reducing per-expert overhead

inlines.text: Reducing per-expert overhead

blocks.text: We reduce per-expert overhead in four ways. First, we improve GEMM and NVLink efficiency by grouping both computation and communication for each expert group. This reduces kernel-launch overhead and tail effects. Second, we reduce host-device synchronization by using device-resident token metadata and initiating all-to-all communication directly from the GPU. Third, we further optimize all-to-all with symmetric memory to exchange tokens directly over NVLink without staging copies, improving communication throughput and reducing HBM contention when running GEMMs concurrently. Lastly, we batch load-balancing loss across layers, replacing per-layer all-reduces with a single batched reduction across all layers. These optimizations enable us to train sparser models without significantly degrading MFU.

blocks.text: Scaling Muon

inlines.text: Scaling Muon

blocks.text: When scaling up to MAI-Base-2, we found that Muon delivered more stable training dynamics and large efficiency gains over AdamW. Adopting Muon for our largest models required reducing its per-step overhead.

inlines.text: When scaling up to MAI-Base-2, we found that Muon delivered more stable training dynamics and large efficiency gains over AdamW. Adopting Muon for our largest models required reducing its per-step overhead.

blocks.text: Muon orthogonalizes the momentum of each weight matrix with Newton–Schulz, an iterative algorithm consisting of several matrix multiplications. This requires the full matrix, which conflicts with ZeRO’s sharding of momentum across the data-parallel dimension. Following prior work, we reshard the momentum during the optimizer step. Each GPU updates its local FP32 momentum shard and casts it to BF16. An all-to-all exchange, batched over parameters of the same shape, then gives each GPU ownership of a subset of full momentum matrices. Each GPU orthogonalizes its full momentum matrices locally with a symmetry-aware Newton–Schulz kernel. A second all-to-all returns the updates to their original shards, where they are cast back to FP32 and applied to the weights.

inlines.text: We further apply several optimizations that are beneficial to our training efficiency on 16K GPUs:
We overlap communication and computation by prefetching multiple batches.
We cache and reuse the resharding metadata to avoid repeated indexing logic. This is especially useful in sparse MoE models with thousands of identically shaped parameters.

Selected weights, such as the MoE router weights, are replicated across GPUs rather than sharded. The first communication phase is skipped, and we instead issue an all-gather collective after Newton-Schulz to get the full set of replicated updates.

blocks.text: After optimizations, Muon accounted for 2.1% (165 ms) of the average training iteration time of MAI-Base-2. We tracked the quality of our implementation and prioritized changes based on profiles, using both large-scale and small-scale testing setups. We compared measurements from tests to the theoretical peak performance, which we estimated to be 55 ms and bottlenecked by communication for MAI-Base-2’s final training setup. We attribute the gap between theoretical and measured performance to stragglers, kernel dispatch overheads, load imbalance, and memory copies/allocations during resharding.

blocks.text: Activation gradient clipping

inlines.text: Activation gradient clipping

blocks.text: Gradient clipping is a common method to stabilize training by reducing the impact of outlier gradients. Standard gradient clipping operates on the global norm of the weight gradient for a whole batch. However, outlier gradients are typically driven by a small portion of the data within a batch. An outlier can therefore cause the gradients from the entire batch to be scaled down, including contributions from otherwise well-behaved examples. As a more targeted mitigation, we clip the gradients of activations at selected places in the network. Together with Muon, this keeps MAI-Base-2’s gradient norm in a much tighter range than MAI-Base-1’s (Figure 7).

Our corpus grew by roughly 36% from MAI-Base-1 to MAI-Base-2, measured in unique training tokens (see Figure 10).

blocks.text: Since MAI-Thinking-1, we’ve improved our quality classification, topic binning, web parsing, deduplication, and evaluation decontamination. For MAI-Base-2, we expanded our pipelines to process substantially more web content1, with a March 2026 knowledge cutoff. We also used embedding-based diversity sampling to prioritize novel data and reduce duplicative content. Our experiments showed that these approaches substantially improved model performance.

blocks.text: Unlike MAI-Base-1, MAI-Base-2 is pre-trained natively with vision using an encoder-free VLM architecture. Accordingly, we invested heavily in growing our VLM corpus across image-text pairs and documents with interleaved text and images. The corpus spans tasks including image captioning from the web, chart understanding, visual grounding, spatial reasoning, medical understanding, computer use, sheet-music reading, and other areas we anticipate users will find useful. Our VLM corpus contains 4.5T unique tokens and, with repetition, VLM data accounted for 18% of the 50T-token training mixture.
